pos: n. (the closed hand; a measure of assault, of false religion, and of God's grasp)
etymology: From Old English fyst, the clenched hand. Scripture uses it three ways — as the instrument of a blow the law must assess, as the emblem of a fast that quarrels, and, in Agur's question, as the figure for the hand that holds the wind.
biblical_def: The law takes the closed hand seriously enough to legislate for it: “And if men strive together, and one smite another with a stone, or with his fist, and he die not, but keepeth his bed” (Exodus 21:18). A stone and a fist are named in one breath, because the law is interested in the harm and not in whether a weapon was picked up. Isaiah then puts the fist inside a religious observance, which is where it does the most damage: “Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high” (Isaiah 58:4). A man can keep a real fast, in the right month, and have his prayer refused because of what his hand is doing to his brother. And Agur takes the same word into an unanswerable question: “Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?” (Proverbs 30:4). The fist that holds the wind is the only fist worth fearing, and the question about His Son's name is answered in the Gospels.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the fist as the hand clenched; the hand with the fingers doubled into the palm.
webster_full: FIST, n. [Sax. fyst.] The hand clenched; the hand with the fingers doubled into the palm.
FIST, v.t. To strike with the fist. To gripe with the fist.
SMITE, v.t. [Sax. smitan.] To strike; to throw, drive or force against, as the fist or hand, a stone or a weapon.
FAST, v.i. To abstain from food, beyond the usual time; to omit to take the usual meals, for a time.
STRIFE, n. Exertion or contention for superiority; contest of emulation, either by intellectual or physical efforts; discord; contention.
scriptures: Exodus 21:18
And if men strive together, and one smite another with a stone, or with his fist, and he die not, but keepeth his bed:
Isaiah 58:4
Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high.
Proverbs 30:4

Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?
I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken me by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark.
corruption_summary: Fasting and other disciplines are treated as devices that oblige God, so that a man may keep the observance and never examine the hand.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 58 is the standing rebuke to every transactional piety. The people are fasting correctly — the chapter grants that they seek God daily and delight to know His ways — and God refuses the fast because of the fist. The mechanism they trusted was: perform the discipline, obtain the hearing. Verse 4 breaks the circuit. Ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high. The rest of the chapter names the fast God chose: loose the bands of wickedness, deal thy bread to the hungry, bring the poor that are cast out to thy house.

The Roman system of merit is the historic large-scale case, and the Reformation named it. But the mechanism is native to the human heart and survives in any congregation. A man in a quarrel with his brother goes on a fast and expects the fast to count; a church raises its intensity in worship while a member's grievance is left unaddressed. Christ made the same point plainer still: leave thy gift before the altar, go thy way, first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer. The fist has to open before the hands are lifted.
roots_summary: Hebrew egroph (H106), a fist; chophen (H2651), the hollow of the hand, a fist; tsum (H6685), a fast; matstsah (H4683), strife.
roots_lines: Hebrew egroph (H106) — a fist; only Exodus 21:18 and Isaiah 58:4, the blow and the fast.
Hebrew chophen (H2651) — the closed hand, a handful; Proverbs 30:4, the wind gathered in his fists.
Hebrew tsom (H6685) — a fast; the observance Isaiah's hearers kept correctly.
Hebrew rib (H7379) — a quarrel, contention; the strife and debate of Isaiah 58:4.
Greek kolaphizo (G2852) — to strike with the fist; Matthew 26:67, what they did to Christ.
usage: “With a stone, or with his fist” — the law weighs the harm, not the weapon.
“The fist of wickedness” — a correct fast with a closed hand.
“Gathered the wind in his fists” — the only fist worth fearing.

pos: n. (the foot of a beast of prey; the deliverance David reckoned on before Goliath)
etymology: From Old French poue, a paw. In 1 Samuel 17 the Hebrew is simply yad, hand — the lion's hand and the bear's hand, set in the same sentence as the hand of the Philistine, so that the three are weighed as one kind of danger.
biblical_def: David's argument before Saul is not about his own ability, and it is not a boast about the past: “David said moreover, The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine. And Saul said unto David, Go, and the LORD be with thee” (1 Samuel 17:37). The Hebrew word is the same for all three — the lion's hand, the bear's hand, the Philistine's hand — so the reasoning is an argument from experience about who does the delivering, not an estimate of the odds. The ground of his confidence is stated in the previous verse and it is theological, not martial: “Thy servant slew both the lion and the bear: and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God” (1 Samuel 17:36). Elsewhere the beasts close in with no deliverance in sight, and the Psalm that says so is the Psalm of the cross: “For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm 22:16). Daniel's vision uses the claw for empire itself: “whose teeth were of iron, and his nails of brass; which devoured, brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with his feet” (Daniel 7:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a paw as the foot of a beast of prey having claws, as the lion, the tiger, the dog, the cat — and the verb, to scrape with the fore foot.
webster_full: PAW, n. [W. pawen.] The foot of a beast of prey having claws, as the lion, the tiger, the dog, the cat, &c.
PAW, v.i. To draw the fore foot along the ground; to scrape with the fore foot.
PAW, v.t. To handle roughly; to scratch; to flatter.
CLAW, n. The sharp hooked nail of a beast, bird or other animal.
DELIVER, v.t. [L. libero.] To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty; to rescue from danger.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 17:37

David said moreover, The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine. And Saul said unto David, Go, and the LORD be with thee.
1 Samuel 17:36
Thy servant slew both the lion and the bear: and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God.
Psalm 22:16
For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.
Daniel 7:19

Then I would know the truth of the fourth beast, which was diverse from all the others, exceeding dreadful, whose teeth were of iron, and his nails of brass; which devoured, brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with his feet;
corruption_summary: David and Goliath is preached as a lesson in self-belief, with the giant recast as whatever obstacle a hearer faces and David as the hearer.
corruption_paragraphs: The motivational reading puts the listener in David's place and makes the story about courage. Verse 36 forbids it. David's stated reason for expecting to win is not that he is brave or skilled but that this Philistine hath defied the armies of the living God — the fight is God's, and David is the one God happens to be using. The lion and the bear are evidence in an argument about the LORD's record, not about David's. A sermon that swaps the subject of the sentence has told the opposite story with the same props.

Psalm 22:16 keeps the reading honest in the other direction, and it is the verse the triumphal version cannot use. There the beasts encircle and no deliverance comes; the hands and feet are pierced. Scripture's Shepherd-King was delivered out of the paw of the lion, and Scripture's greater Son was not — because He was the offering. Any doctrine promising the believer David's outcome in every trial has to explain Psalm 22, and the explanation is that the Son endured the beasts so that His people could be raised out of them at the last.
roots_summary: Hebrew yad (H3027), hand, paw; ari (H738), a lion; dob (H1677), a bear; Aramaic tephar (H2953), a nail, claw.
roots_lines: Hebrew yad (H3027) — hand; used of the lion, the bear, and the Philistine alike in 1 Samuel 17:37.
Hebrew ari (H738) — a lion; 1 Peter 5:8 keeps the figure for the adversary.
Hebrew dob (H1677) — a bear; the second of David's witnesses.
Hebrew keleb (H3611) — a dog; Psalm 22:16, the pack that compassed the Sufferer.
Aramaic tephar (H2953) — nail, claw; Daniel 7:19, the fourth beast's nails of brass.
usage: “Out of the paw of the lion” — evidence about the LORD, not about David.
“He hath defied the armies of the living God” — whose quarrel it actually is.
“Dogs have compassed me” — the encirclement with no rescue.

pos: n. (body armour of linked or scaled metal; Goliath's coat and Saul's loan)
etymology: From Latin macula, a mesh or spot, through Old French maille. The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 17:5 is shiryon qasqassim — a coat of scales — describing armour built like a fish, each plate overlapping the next.
biblical_def: Goliath is introduced by inventory, and the weight is part of the intimidation: “And he had an helmet of brass upon his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of brass” (1 Samuel 17:5). Roughly a hundred and twenty-five pounds of scaled bronze, and it covered everything the sling would later find except the forehead. Saul's response to the challenge is to offer David the same category of protection — his own armour and a coat of mail — which David put on, found he could not walk in, and took off. The armour of a king who would not fight was no use to the boy who would. Chronicles shows a godly king equipping his army properly: “And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones” (2 Chronicles 26:14) — and the same Uzziah was struck with leprosy when he presumed to burn incense, so that competence in arms proved no license in worship. Paul takes the whole vocabulary into the Christian's warfare: “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11). The mail a believer wears is not his own and it fits.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mail as a coat of steel net-work, formerly worn for defending the body against swords, poniards, &c. — and in general, armor; that which defends the body.
webster_full: MAIL, n. [Fr. maille, a stitch or mesh; L. macula, a spot or mesh.] A coat of steel net-work, formerly worn for defending the body against swords, poniards, &c.
MAIL, n. Armor; that which defends the body.
HABERGEON, n. A coat of mail; a breastplate; armor to defend the neck and breast.
HELMET, n. A defensive armor for the head; a head-piece; a morion.
BRASS, n. An alloy of copper and zinc; in Scripture, commonly copper or bronze.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 17:5
And he had an helmet of brass upon his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of brass.
2 Chronicles 26:14
And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones.
Ephesians 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
1 Samuel 17:37

David said moreover, The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine. And Saul said unto David, Go, and the LORD be with thee.
corruption_summary: Spiritual warfare is treated either as a technique for controlling unseen powers or as a metaphor with no real enemy behind it, and Paul's armour is emptied from both directions.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 6 has been made the charter of a whole industry of territorial rebuking and formulaic prayers, and Paul's actual pieces do not support it. Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer — every one of them is a doctrine or a duty already given to an ordinary Christian. The verb repeated through the passage is stand, not advance or bind. A believer in the armour is not conducting operations; he is holding ground that Christ has already taken.

The opposite corruption is to hear the whole passage as figurative encouragement with no devil in it. Paul names the wiles of the devil and principalities and powers, and the 1689 confesses the reality of Satan and his angels. What Scripture will not grant is either fear or fascination. Saul's coat of mail is the standing parable: borrowed defences that fit another man and hinder this one. David went with five stones and a name — the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel — and that is the armour Ephesians 6 actually describes.
roots_summary: Hebrew shiryon (H8302), a coat of mail, breastplate; qasqeseth (H7193), a scale; nesheq (H5402), weaponry; Greek panoplia (G3833), full armour.
roots_lines: Hebrew shiryon (H8302) — a coat of mail; 1 Samuel 17:5, 38 and Isaiah 59:17 of the LORD Himself.
Hebrew qasqeseth (H7193) — a scale, as of a fish; Goliath's coat was built of them.
Hebrew shiryon as habergeon — 2 Chronicles 26:14, Uzziah's issue to the host.
Greek panoplia (G3833) — the whole armour; Ephesians 6:11, 13.
Greek histemi (G2476) — to stand; the repeated verb of Ephesians 6, not to advance.
usage: “The weight of the coat was five thousand shekels” — the inventory as intimidation.
“Put on the whole armour of God” — every piece a doctrine already given.
Saul's coat on David — borrowed defences that fit another man.

pos: n. (the distance an arrow flies; the space Hagar put between herself and her dying son)
etymology: From bow + shot — the range of an arrow, roughly a hundred yards, used as an informal measure of distance. The KJV uses it once, at Genesis 21:16, and the measure is doing pastoral work: far enough not to watch, near enough to hear.
biblical_def: The water is gone, the boy is under a shrub, and Hagar does the arithmetic of a mother who has run out: “And she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child. And she sat over against him, and lift up her voice, and wept” (Genesis 21:16). A bowshot is exactly the distance chosen — she will not leave, and she will not watch. What follows corrects her twice over: “And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is” (Genesis 21:17). She had gone where she could not see; God had not. And the deliverance is not a creation but an opening of eyes: “And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink” (Genesis 21:19). The well was within a bowshot the whole time. Hagar had already given God a name for this: “And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?” (Genesis 16:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives bowshot as the space which an arrow may pass when shot from a bow.
webster_full: BOWSHOT, n. The space which an arrow may pass when shot from a bow.
BOW, n. An instrument of war and hunting, made of wood or other elastic matter, with a string fastened to each end.
SHOT, n. The act of shooting; the flight of a missive weapon; also, the distance passed by a missive weapon.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
BOTTLE, n. [Fr. bouteille.] A hollow vessel of glass, wood, leather or other material, with a narrow mouth, for holding liquors.
scriptures: Genesis 21:16

And she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child. And she sat over against him, and lift up her voice, and wept.
Genesis 21:17
And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.
Genesis 21:19
And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink.
Genesis 16:13
And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?
corruption_summary: Hagar is treated as a footnote in Abraham's story, when Scripture gives her two direct encounters with God and lets her name Him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The neglect is the church's own. Hagar is an Egyptian slave woman, used and then sent away, and she receives what almost no one else in Genesis receives: the angel of the LORD seeking her out twice in a wilderness, and the liberty to name God. Genesis 16:13 is the only place in Scripture where a human being gives God a name, and the one who does it is her. The principle to recover is that the God of the covenant line is not indifferent to the people that line mistreated.

The mechanics of the rescue are worth dwelling on. God does not make a well; He opens her eyes to one that was already inside the bowshot she had measured. Distress narrows sight before it narrows supply, and a great deal of Christian despair is of exactly this kind — the provision is at hand and the eyes are shut. Note also that God heard the lad, not the mother, though the mother was the one weeping aloud. Heaven's attention is not distributed by volume.
roots_summary: Hebrew metachave qesheth (H2909 + H7198), a bowshot; shama (H8085), to hear; paqach (H6491), to open the eyes; roi (H7210), seeing.
roots_lines: Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — a bow; the measure of distance in Genesis 21:16.
Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear; the root of Ishmael, God heareth.
Hebrew paqach (H6491) — to open the eyes; Genesis 21:19, the whole miracle.
Hebrew El Roi (H410 + H7210) — the God who sees me; Hagar's name for Him, Genesis 16:13.
Hebrew beer (H875) — a well; within the bowshot the entire time.
usage: “As it were a bowshot” — too far to watch, near enough to stay.
“God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is” — where she could not look.
“God opened her eyes” — the well was there already.

pos: n. pl. (troops armed with the spear; the escort that carried Paul out of Jerusalem)
etymology: From spear + men. At Acts 23:23 the Greek is dexiolaboi, literally right-hand-takers — a rare military term, probably javelin-men or lictors. At Psalm 68:30 the Hebrew is chayyath qaneh, the beast of the reeds.
biblical_def: Forty men have sworn to eat nothing until Paul is dead: “And when it was day, certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul” (Acts 23:12). The Roman chief captain, learning of it from Paul's nephew, responds with overwhelming force: “And he called unto him two centurions, saying, Make ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, and horsemen threescore and ten, and spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night” (Acts 23:23). Four hundred and seventy men, marched at nine in the evening, to move one prisoner. Luke records the numbers because they are the shape of a promise kept: the night before, “the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul: for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome” (Acts 23:11). God had said Rome, and the Roman army became the means. The Psalmist prays against the same class of power where it is hostile: “Rebuke the company of spearmen, the multitude of the bulls, with the calves of the people, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war” (Psalm 68:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a spearman as one who is armed with a spear; and a spear as a long pointed weapon used in war and hunting.
webster_full: SPEARMAN, n. One who is armed with a spear.
SPEAR, n. [Sax. spere.] A long, pointed weapon, used in war and hunting, by thrusting or throwing; a lance.
CENTURION, n. [L. centurio, from centum, a hundred.] In the Roman armies, a military officer who commanded a hundred men.
ESCORT, n. [Fr. escorte.] A guard; a body of armed men which attends an officer, or baggage, provisions or munitions, to protect them.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town, to defend it.
scriptures: Acts 23:23
And he called unto him two centurions, saying, Make ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, and horsemen threescore and ten, and spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night;
Acts 23:12
And when it was day, certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul.
Acts 23:11
And the night following the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul: for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome.
Psalm 68:30
Rebuke the company of spearmen, the multitude of the bulls, with the calves of the people, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war.
corruption_summary: Providence is expected to arrive by miracle, so that the ordinary machinery God actually uses — a nephew who overhears, an officer who follows procedure — is not recognized as the answer.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 23 is a small masterclass in how God usually keeps His word. The Lord promises Rome on one night; the deliverance the next day comes through a boy who happened to hear something, a centurion who took him seriously, and a garrison commander protecting a Roman citizen because the law required it. Not one of those men was a believer, and not one step of it was miraculous. A Christian waiting for the spectacular can live through an entire answered prayer and file it under coincidence.

The chapter also settles a question about the state. Paul accepts a pagan army's protection without apology, as he had invoked his citizenship at Philippi and would appeal to Caesar later. The magistrate bears the sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of them that do well, and a Christian may lawfully use that protection. Psalm 68:30 holds the other half: the same power, turned hostile and delighting in war, is something to pray against. Neither reverence nor contempt for the sword; a doctrine of it.
roots_summary: Greek dexiolabos (G1187), a spearman, right-hand-taker; stratiotes (G4757), a soldier; hekatontarches (G1543), a centurion; Hebrew qaneh (H7070), a reed.
roots_lines: Greek dexiolabos (G1187) — spearman; a rare word, only Acts 23:23.
Greek hekatontarches (G1543) — a centurion; two of them detailed for one prisoner.
Greek anathematizo (G332) — to bind under a curse; the forty men's oath, Acts 23:12.
Hebrew chayyath qaneh (H2416 + H7070) — the beast of the reeds; Psalm 68:30, rendered company of spearmen.
Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness; the errand the escort was serving, Acts 23:11.
usage: “Spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night” — the shape of a promise kept.
“So must thou bear witness also at Rome” — said the night before.
“Scatter thou the people that delight in war” — the same power, prayed against.

pos: n. pl. (archers; the arm of an army whose noise empties a city)
etymology: From bow + men. The Hebrew is romeh qesheth, casters of the bow — archers. The bow is the ranged weapon of the ancient world, and Scripture regularly makes it the emblem of a strength that can fail at a distance from the enemy.
biblical_def: Jeremiah describes an invasion by its sound: “The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks: every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein” (Jeremiah 4:29). The archers do not need to arrive; their noise empties the towns. The same prophet later turns the bow against the great empire itself: “Put yourselves in array against Babylon round about: all ye that bend the bow, shoot at her, spare no arrows: for she hath sinned against the LORD” (Jeremiah 50:14). Chronicles records the skill at its height in Israel, and it was formidable: “They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 12:2) — ambidextrous Benjamite archers, the elite of David's outlaw band. And the Psalmist records the same arm in failure, with the reason given in the next verse: “The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle” (Psalm 78:9). They were armed and they turned back, because they kept not the covenant of God and refused to walk in His law. Equipment was never the variable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bowman as a man who uses a bow; an archer.
webster_full: BOWMAN, n. A man who uses a bow; an archer.
ARCHER, n. [Fr. archer, from L. arcus, a bow.] One who uses a bow; a bowman; one who shoots with a bow.
BOW, n. An instrument of war and hunting, made of wood or other elastic matter, with a string fastened to each end.
QUIVER, n. A case or sheath for arrows.
ARRAY, v.t. To place or dispose in order, as troops for battle.
scriptures: Jeremiah 4:29
The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks: every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein.
Jeremiah 50:14
Put yourselves in array against Babylon round about: all ye that bend the bow, shoot at her, spare no arrows: for she hath sinned against the LORD.
1 Chronicles 12:2
They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin.
Psalm 78:9
The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle.
corruption_summary: Failure in the day of battle is diagnosed as a want of preparation, when the Psalmist attributes it to a covenant not kept by men who were fully armed.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 78:9 is a verse the competent find uncomfortable. Ephraim was armed. Ephraim carried bows. Ephraim turned back. The psalm supplies the reason across the next three verses — they kept not the covenant of God, refused to walk in his law, and forgot his works — and none of the three is a training deficiency. A church can be doctrinally equipped, historically informed, and institutionally sound, and turn back, and the deficiency will not be found in the armoury.

Jeremiah 50:14 supplies the other half of the doctrine and keeps it from fatalism. Babylon is to be shot at, with no arrows spared, because she hath sinned against the LORD — God's judgment on an empire arrives through men who bend actual bows. Providence does not cancel means; it employs them. The Benjamite archers of 1 Chronicles 12:2 are described with real admiration for real skill. Scripture is not embarrassed by competence. It simply refuses to make competence the thing that decides the day.

Hebrew darak qesheth (H1869) — to tread the bow, i.e. to bend it by foot; Jeremiah 50:14.
Hebrew chets (H2671) — an arrow; Psalm 127:4, children as arrows in the hand.
Hebrew nashaq (H5401) — to be armed, equipped; Psalm 78:9, Ephraim armed and turning back.
usage: “The noise of the horsemen and bowmen” — the sound alone empties the towns.
“Being armed, and carrying bows, turned back” — equipment was not the variable.
“Spare no arrows: for she hath sinned against the LORD” — judgment through means.

pos: n. (weapons in general; in the KJV, Jonathan's bow and arrows)
etymology: From Old French artillerie, implements of war, long before gunpowder. The KJV uses it once, at 1 Samuel 20:40, of Jonathan's bow and arrows — a clear instance of a word that has narrowed since 1611 and now misleads a modern reader.
biblical_def: The arrows were a signal. Jonathan had arranged to shoot beyond a boy and let what he called to the lad tell David, hidden in the field, whether Saul meant to kill him. When the message has been delivered, the weapons have served their purpose and are sent away: “And Jonathan gave his artillery unto his lad, and said unto him, Go, carry them to the city” (1 Samuel 20:40). With the boy gone, the two men could meet in the open, and what follows is a covenant rather than a plan of escape: “And Jonathan said to David, Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, The LORD be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever. And he arose and departed: and Jonathan went into the city” (1 Samuel 20:42). Jonathan is the crown prince, and the man he is protecting will have his throne; the covenant he swears costs him a kingdom and he swears it anyway. The weapons in the story are the same kind Chronicles lists in a national armoury — “shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones” (2 Chronicles 26:14) — and here they are used to carry a word between friends.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines artillery as offensive weapons of war; and notes that formerly the word comprehended all sorts of weapons and engines used in war, as in 1 Samuel 20, where it denotes Jonathan's bow and arrows.
webster_full: ARTILLERY, n. [Fr. artillerie, from artiller, to fortify.] In a general sense, offensive weapons of war. Hence it was formerly used for bows and arrows.
ARTILLERY, n. Cannon; great guns; ordnance, including guns, mortars and howitzers, with their furniture.
ARTILLERY, n. The men who manage cannon and mortars.
ORDNANCE, n. Cannon or great guns, mortars and howitzers; artillery.
COVENANT, n. [L. con and venio, to come together.] A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 20:40
And Jonathan gave his artillery unto his lad, and said unto him, Go, carry them to the city.
1 Samuel 20:42

And Jonathan said to David, Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, The LORD be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever. And he arose and departed: and Jonathan went into the city.
2 Chronicles 26:14
And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones.
1 Samuel 17:5
And he had an helmet of brass upon his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of brass.
corruption_summary: A word that has narrowed since 1611 is read with its modern sense, and the archaic vocabulary of the Authorized Version is then blamed for the reader's confusion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The difficulty is linguistic and honest. Artillery in 1611 meant implements of war of any kind, and only later narrowed to cannon; Webster still gives both senses in 1828 and cites this very verse. A reader who does not know that pictures field guns in the reign of Saul. The principle to recover is that the remedy for an archaic word is a dictionary and not a shrug — a reader who looks up one word per chapter will in a year read the Authorized Version with ease.

The dictionary is KJV-honoring and not KJV-only, and this entry is a fair illustration of why both halves matter. The Authorized Version's vocabulary is exact, dignified, and occasionally three centuries away from the reader; that is a cost, and it is paid by study rather than by abandoning the text. Jonathan's covenant in verse 42 is worth the small labour. A king's son swore, in the name of the LORD, to protect the man who would take his crown, and kept the oath at the cost of everything a prince could lose.
roots_summary: Hebrew keli (H3627), instruments, implements, weapons; qesheth (H7198), a bow; berith (H1285), a covenant.

Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — a bow; the actual weapon in Jonathan's hand.
Hebrew chets (H2671) — an arrow; the three shot beyond the lad as a signal.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant; sworn between Jonathan and David in the LORD's name.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace; Go in peace, the last word between them in the field.
usage: “Jonathan gave his artillery unto his lad” — a bow and arrows, not cannon.
“The LORD be between me and thee” — the covenant that cost a kingdom.
“Go in peace” — said by the prince to the man who would replace him.

pos: adj. (furnished with backward points; of the irons that cannot take leviathan)
etymology: From Latin barba, a beard, through Old French barbe — the backward-facing point on a hook or harpoon that prevents withdrawal. Job 41:7 uses it of the fishing irons that would be useless against leviathan.
biblical_def: The LORD's final speech to Job is a series of questions about a creature Job cannot handle, and the barbs are part of the mockery: “Canst thou fill his skin with barbed irons? or his head with fish spears?” (Job 41:7). Barbed irons are the whaler's tools, made so that what goes in will not come out; against leviathan they are a joke. The point is not zoological. God has spent two chapters demonstrating that Job cannot master a single beast in the creation, and therefore has no standing to summon its Maker to account for the government of the world. Job's own complaint had used the language of a target set up to be shot at: “I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken me by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark” (Job 16:12). He felt barbed. God's answer does not explain the suffering — not one word of the divine speeches addresses the wager in chapter 1 — and Job repents in dust and ashes anyway, having seen the One who governs. The imagery of the weapon whetted and aimed belongs finally to God alone: “If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me” (Deuteronomy 32:41).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines barbed as bearded, or jagged with hooks or points — as a barbed arrow; furnished with barbs.
webster_full: BARBED, pp. Bearded; jagged with hooks or points; as a barbed arrow.
BARB, n. [L. barba, a beard.] The points that stand backward in an arrow, fish-hook or other instrument for piercing, intended to prevent its being extracted.
HARPOON, n. A harping iron; a spear or javelin, used to strike whales for killing them.
LEVIATHAN, n. [Heb.] An aquatic animal, described in the book of Job, ch. xli, and mentioned in other passages of Scripture.
MARK, n. A thing set up to be aimed at; a butt; the object at which a missile is directed.
scriptures: Job 41:7
Canst thou fill his skin with barbed irons? or his head with fish spears?
I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken me by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark.
Deuteronomy 32:41
If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me.
Psalm 22:16
For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.
corruption_summary: The divine speeches are read as an evasion — overwhelming a sufferer with power instead of answering him — when their argument is about who is competent to govern.
corruption_paragraphs: A common modern reading finds Job 38 to 41 unsatisfying: the man asked why, and God talked about ostriches and sea monsters. But the question Job had actually raised by the end was not why so much as who — he had summoned God to court, and demanded an umpire. The speeches answer that question exactly. A man who cannot put a hook in leviathan's jaw is not qualified to review the moral administration of the universe, and Job, who was the wisest man in the argument, concedes it in eight verses without ever learning about the wager.

The book's harder mercy is that Job's complaint is never rebuked as sin. He had said God set him up for a mark, shaken him to pieces, broken him asunder — and in chapter 42 it is the friends, with all their careful orthodoxy, of whom God says ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. The sufferer who argued with God was nearer the truth than the theologians who defended Him with a false account. Scripture permits a man to be barbed and to say so.
roots_summary: Hebrew sukkah (H7905), barbed irons, harpoons; livyathan (H3882), leviathan; mattarah (H4307), a mark, target; chereb (H2719), a sword.
roots_lines: Hebrew sukkoth (H7905) — barbed irons, harpoons; only Job 41:7.

Hebrew livyathan (H3882) — leviathan; the creature no tackle will hold.
Hebrew mattarah (H4307) — a mark to shoot at; Job 16:12, set me up for his mark.
Hebrew chets (H2671) — an arrow; Job 6:4, the arrows of the Almighty within him.
usage: “Canst thou fill his skin with barbed irons?” — the whaler's tools, and useless.
“Set me up for his mark” — how the sufferer described it, and was not rebuked.
“If I whet my glittering sword” — the weapon that belongs to God alone.

pos: v. (pierced by a horn; the case that founds the law of the dangerous thing)
etymology: From Old English gar, a spear. Exodus 21 uses it of an ox that kills with its horn, and the case becomes the Bible's foundational teaching on liability for a danger a man knows about and does not restrain.
biblical_def: The law states the simple case first: “If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die: then the ox shall be surely stoned, and his flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be quit” (Exodus 21:28). The animal is destroyed because a life was taken and Genesis 9 requires a reckoning even from beasts; the owner goes free, because he could not have known. Then the case turns on knowledge. Where the ox had a history and the owner had been warned and kept no guard, the owner is tried for the death himself. And the statute refuses to let the victim's status alter the verdict: “Whether he have gored a son, or have gored a daughter, according to this judgment shall it be done unto him” (Exodus 21:31). A daughter's death is worth exactly what a son's is, which was not the settled opinion of the ancient world. The principle runs with the building code a chapter later — “When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a battlement for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence” (Deuteronomy 22:8) — and both stand under the commandment that values the image of God: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man” (Genesis 9:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gore, as a verb, to stab; to pierce; to penetrate with a pointed instrument, as a spear — and notes it is said of animals that pierce with horns.
webster_full: GORE, v.t. To stab; to pierce; to penetrate with a pointed instrument, as a spear.
GORE, v.t. To pierce with the horns; as, an ox gores a man.
GORE, n. [Sax. gor.] Blood; but generally, thick or clotted blood; blood that after effusion becomes inspissated.
LIABLE, a. [Fr. lier, to bind.] Answerable; responsible; bound to make satisfaction or atonement.
QUIT, a. Free; clear; discharged from; absolved.
scriptures: Exodus 21:28
If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die: then the ox shall be surely stoned, and his flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be quit.
Exodus 21:31
Whether he have gored a son, or have gored a daughter, according to this judgment shall it be done unto him.
Deuteronomy 22:8
When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a battlement for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence.
Genesis 9:6
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
corruption_summary: The case laws of Exodus are dismissed as primitive, when their reasoning about knowledge, warning, and responsibility is more exact than most of what replaced it.
corruption_paragraphs: The goring ox is a standing exhibit for the claim that the Mosaic law is a crude relic. Read closely it is the opposite. The statute distinguishes the unforeseeable accident from the known hazard; it makes the decisive factor a warning the owner received and ignored; it destroys the animal because a human life was taken and human life is not on a level with animal life; and it holds a man accountable for a death his negligence permitted. Every serious system of liability since has been working out the same distinctions, usually less clearly.

Verse 31 is the quiet revolution. Ancient codes commonly scaled a penalty to the victim's rank, and some prescribed that a man whose ox killed another man's daughter should surrender his own — punishing an innocent. Exodus refuses both: the same judgment for a son and a daughter, and the guilt stays with the guilty. That is Genesis 9:6 worked into a statute. Where a life is valued by its economic yield or its social standing, this verse is the rebuke, and it is over three thousand years old.

“In the image of God made he man” — why a beast is destroyed for it.

pos: v.t. (to wave a weapon so that it is seen; of the LORD's sword before the nations)
etymology: From Old French brandir, from brand, a sword-blade. To brandish is to display a weapon rather than to strike with it — the act is aimed at the eye, and Ezekiel uses it exactly so.
biblical_def: Ezekiel's oracle against Egypt describes a judgment whose first work is done by sight: “Yea, I will make many people amazed at thee, and their kings shall be horribly afraid for thee, when I shall brandish my sword before them; and they shall tremble at every moment, every man for his own life, in the day of thy fall” (Ezekiel 32:10). The sword is drawn and shown, and the watching kings are undone by what happened to someone else — every man for his own life. The fall of one nation is a sermon to the others. The verse before names the intent: “I will also vex the hearts of many people, when I shall bring thy destruction among the nations, into the countries which thou hast not known” (Ezekiel 32:9). The same drawn blade appears in the Song of Moses, where God claims vengeance as His own prerogative: “If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me” (Deuteronomy 32:41). Between the whetting and the falling there is a space, and that space is mercy — the warning given in time for a nation to repent, which is precisely why the sword is brandished before it is used.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brandish as to move or wave, as a weapon; to raise and move in various directions; to shake or flourish.
webster_full: BRANDISH, v.t. [Fr. brandir, from brand, a sword.] To move or wave, as a weapon; to raise and move in various directions; to shake or flourish; as, to brandish a sword or a cane.
BRANDISH, v.t. To play with; to flourish; as, to brandish syllogisms.
BRAND, n. A sword, so called from its glittering or brightness.
WHET, v.t. [Sax. hwettan.] To rub for the purpose of sharpening; to sharpen by attrition; as, to whet a knife.
VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense; retribution.
scriptures: Ezekiel 32:10

Yea, I will make many people amazed at thee, and their kings shall be horribly afraid for thee, when I shall brandish my sword before them; and they shall tremble at every moment, every man for his own life, in the day of thy fall.
Ezekiel 32:9
I will also vex the hearts of many people, when I shall bring thy destruction among the nations, into the countries which thou hast not known.
Deuteronomy 32:41
If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies, and will reward them that hate me.
Jeremiah 50:14
Put yourselves in array against Babylon round about: all ye that bend the bow, shoot at her, spare no arrows: for she hath sinned against the LORD.
corruption_summary: Judgment on the nations is treated as an embarrassment of the Old Testament, and the warning function of the drawn sword — a mercy, given before the stroke — is lost with it.
corruption_paragraphs: A God who brandishes a sword offends the modern instinct, and the offence is usually managed by assigning these oracles to an earlier and harsher stage of religion. The New Testament will not permit the division. The same Lord who wept over Jerusalem told it precisely what was coming and when, and Revelation's bowls are not gentler than Ezekiel's sword. What Scripture presents is one God, whose judgments on nations are announced at length, in public, and in advance.

The pastoral weight of the word is in the delay it implies. Brandishing is not striking. Deuteronomy 32:41 puts a whetting before the taking hold on judgment, and Ezekiel has the sword shown to watching kings before it falls on any of them. Jonah went to Nineveh with forty days and no offer of terms, and Nineveh repented, and God relented, and the prophet was angry about it. Every announced judgment in Scripture is an unspent interval. The nation that hears the blade drawn and does not turn has been warned in the only way a God of mercy warns.

Hebrew chereb (H2719) — a sword; the standing figure of God's judgment on nations.
Hebrew latash (H3913) — to whet, sharpen; Deuteronomy 32:41, the glittering sword.
Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge; vengeance claimed by God, quoted at Romans 12:19.
Hebrew charad (H2729) — to tremble; Ezekiel 32:10, every man for his own life.
usage: “When I shall brandish my sword before them” — shown before it falls.
“Every man for his own life” — another nation's fall, preached to the watchers.
“If I whet my glittering sword” — and the whetting takes time.
